title: Data Visualization
text:
These visualizations are reflective of the data compiled from the first nineteen objects that were submitted to You Can Begin Again. The most commonly-used set of pronouns for participants was “he/him” at 33%, followed by “they/them” at 19%, “she/her” and “he/they” at 14%, “she/they” at 10%, and finally “any” pronouns and “neopronouns” at only 5% of participants (See Fig. 1).



Figure 1. This is a pie chart of the distribution of the pronouns of those who submitted to the archive.


There is, however, an interesting shift as one starts to look at the pronouns that participants assigned to their self-made avatars (See Fig. 2). Despite “he/him” pronouns only being used by 33% of the archive’s participants, almost 50% gave their player characters (PCs) “he/him” pronouns. The second most common category is “they/them,” which almost doubled from its initial 19% to be assigned to 32% of archive participants’ PCs. The amount of people who utilized multiple pronoun sets (he/they, she/they, any pronouns) also reduced significantly, which is reflective of the fact that players are generally restricted to selecting one binary set of pronouns (he/him, they/them, she/her) in most standard character creators instead of being able to write their own or select multiple. This restriction can be understood as a result of the cost of recording multiple variations of character dialogue that are referring to the player character with each pronoun set.



Figure 2. This is a pie chart depicting the different pronouns that submitters used for their self-made video game avatars


This coincides with data on whether or not player’s self-selected pronouns were congruent with the pronouns they assigned their avatars (See Fig. 3). Participants that use “he/him” were more likely than any other group to use the same set of pronouns for their player characters, while every other group was more likely to pick a set that did not match the pronouns that they use for themselves. On the other hand, participants who either used multiple sets of pronouns or any pronouns (including neopronouns) almost unilaterally did not give their player characters the same pronouns that they use for themselves. Only one participant, who uses “she/they” pronouns, broke away from this trend and also assigned “she/they” pronouns to her virtual avatar.



Figure 3. This is a pie chart depicting the different pronouns that submitters used for themselves and whether or not they matched

title: Data Visualization
text:
Games
Out of all of the avatars to the archive, the most popular games for them to be made in were Baldur’s Gate III, with 5 submissions, and Stardew Valley, with 3 submissions. The rest of the games represented in the archive only have one associated submission (See Fig. 4.).
 Another thing of note is that the vast majority of these games are either single-player only or allow for solo play. Only three games - Sea of Thieves, Team Fortress 2, and Runescape: Dragonwilds - are solely multiplayer. Most games represented within the archive are also characterized by their narratives, with only the three aforementioned multiplayer games and Minecraft not containing some kind of ‘story mode’ for players to engage with. This reflects the larger trend of narrative-based games incorporating character customization mechanics as a means of encouraging immersion and the player’s embodiment into their characters.

title: About the Archive
text: You Can Begin Again was born out of the experiences of a little boy who didn’t know he was a boy sitting down to play Obsidian Entertainment’s Fallout: New Vegas for the first time. As what the trans community colloquially calls a ‘baby trans,’ my cobbled-together performances of masculinity were kept sequestered to the world of video games as I created my very first Courier Six: ‘Atlas.’ I was addicted from the first time an in-game character referred to me as male. It wasn’t before long that Atlas shrugged the world off his shoulders and morphed into ‘Cain’ in Fallout 3 and Far Cry 5, then ‘Cato’ for a few campaigns of Dungeons and Dragons, and finally ‘Isaac’ when I inevitably returned to the Mojave Wasteland to begin again. In many ways, that makes this work auto-ethnographic; it is a collection of other trans people’s experiences as much as it is directly reflective of my own.

title: About the Archive
text:
Methods
This website was generated under minimal computing princples through Quarto.
Submissions were collected through [a virtual survey]((https://virginiatech.questionpro.com/youcanbeginagaindigitalarchivesubmissions) that was shared in queer-aligned spaces in Blacksburg, Virginia. Participants were also recruited on trans-aligned Discord and Reddit spaces.
When submitting, gamers were asked:

To assign themselves a pseudonym
To state their preferred pronouns
To provide pronouns for their submitted avatars
To say what game their submission came from

They were then asked the following questions:

Why did you choose the game that your character is from?
How do you understand the relationship between the character submitted and your own gender identity and exploration?

title: About the Archive
text:
Constructive Limitations
This archive, like the people whose stories it contains, is both a product of and a response to its surroundings. Because it was primarily shared within Virginia Tech spaces, a limitation of the project is that the archive’s submissions over-represent the experiences of college-educated trans adults that are currently living in or have lived in rural Virginia. Consequently, as Virginia Tech is a primarily-white institution, the stories of white trans people are also more represented; future versions of this archive aim to recruit and platform the stories of more black and brown trans people of color.
The version of this project that exists now is also a response to limitations related to time, labor, and financial support being externally enforced upon it, which is to say that it must adhere to cissexist methods of constructing knowledge environments in order to come into being.
In that sense, it also takes inspiration from Dr. K.J Rawson’s Digital Transgender Archive in that this project acknowledges the constraints forced upon it and has resolved to prioritize the “increased open access to trans history” in order to “complicate(s) normative histories” of gender-diverse and trans experiences in video game spaces.1 Future iterations of this archive aspire to draw elements of the embodied presentation of knowledge present in Danielle Braithwaite Shirley’s Black Trans Archive, which forces users to reckon with the humanity of its archival objects through the usage of an avatar creation system.
You Can Begin Again, on the other hand, is much earlier in its transition. It has taken the plunge – changing its name, buying new clothes, acquiring its first prescription – but it is still in the early stages of becoming something new. It is intimately aware of the limitations that it faces and the cis scrutiny it will inevitably encounter. Still, it does its best to stand as proudly as it can, donned in shades of pink, white, and blue. Please forgive the awkward cracks in its voice; it is still trying to find it.

title: Key Terms
text: These terms establish a foundation for how concepts and ideas for transgender, gender-questioning, and gender-diverse individuals are understood. They also define key video game terminology and the concept of performance.

title: Key Terms
text:
Gender and Identity
Gender Identity: a person’s internal sense of their gender (or lack thereof), which may or may not align with the sex they were coercively assigned at birth.
Transgender: a person who does not identify as the sex that they were coercively assigned at birth.
Cisgender: a person who does identify as the sex that they were coercively assigned at birth.
Gender-Diverse: an umbrella label that encompasses transgender, intersex, and gender-questioning individuals. It also includes Indigenous-specific gender identities.
Gender-Questioning: a person who is questioning or otherwise unsure of whether or not they identify with the sex that they were coercively assigned at birth.
Gender Exploration: the process of learning about your gender identity through things including but not limited to appearance, presentation (in real life or online), “trying out” societal norms and visual indicators of gender and sex, etc.
Gender Dysphoria: an innate feeling of ‘wrongness’ spawned by a mismatch between one’s identity and the gender that they were coercively-assigned gender at birth that can trigger dissociation, depression, anxiety, and suicidality.
Gender Performance: as spearheaded by Judith Butler in Gender Trouble, it is the act of staging, acting-out, and accomplishing (or attempting to accomplish) a concept, ideal, story, or belief of what a gender “should” look and act like based on hegemonic, cissexist, and misogynistic matrices of power. These performances are policed legislatively and socially.
Neopronouns: third-person pronouns that exist outside of normatively-used ones like he/him, she/her, and they/them. While there are historical examples of the usage of neopronouns, in contemporary times they are most often used by nonbinary individuals as a means of expressing their identities in new, and often non-gendered, ways. More popular examples of neopronouns include “ze/hir” and “ey/em.”

title: Key Terms
text:
Video Games and Performance
Role-Playing Games: games, both digital and physical, that involve a player or a group of players pretending to be characters that they are not in a fictional setting and storyline.
Single-Player Games: games that are played offline, where only one individual player is able to interact with, change, and “play” the game. The challenges faced by the player are generated by computer-controlled plot points, world-building, characters, and enemies. They are often more centered around story.
Multi-Player Games: games that are played with others, either online or alongside them in the same room, where multiple players are able to interact with, change, and “play” the game. This genre of video game typically incorporates some kind of competitive and/or interpersonal element.
Ludology: the study of playing games. Within the context of video game studies, this involves an analysis of gameplay systems that allow players to engage and interact with the games themselves; it’s how players “play.”

title: Tenets
text:
By accessing the data and objects contained within this digital project, I agree to the following:

I understand that this is a pro-trans archive that is representative of the vast and varying experiences of trans-identifying people across cultural, racial, and neurodivergent experiences.
I acknowledge that the archival ‘objects’ contained within this collection are not true objects, but are representative of deeply-personal and emotionally-entangled experiences of gender and presentation. I commit to protecting and promoting the humanity of not just the stories contained within this archive, but for all trans people in general.
I will not label or prescribe an identity or an experience on the submissions contained within this archive. I understand that experiences of gender and gender presentation are individualized and that it is not my place to say what someone is or is not.
If I use this data, I will acknowledge the above tenets in writing and will provide proper attribution to the archive and/or this repository of data.

text:

title: Archiving Transgender Worldmaking and Identity Performance in Video Games
text:
Figure 1. A screenshot from Obsidian Entertainment’s 2008 video game, Fallout: New Vegas’, taken during DLC entitled “Dead Money.” The image is of an in-game poster that reads “A chance to begin again!”


Searching for an outlet, many trans people find themselves drawn to video games as a form of escape from the threat of transphobic vitriol and gender-policing in the real world. The avatars that they make then become critical avenues of research for the ways in which they can assist in the exploration of gender identity. Through an intermingling of Judith Butler’s idea of performative gender in Gender Trouble, Sarah Ahmend’s Queer Phenomenology, and Uri Miller’s Embodied Avatars, this project understands the act of playing video games with a self-made avatar as a co-creationary performance of the self, in which trans gamers utilize their player characters to begin again.
You Can Begin Again is a digital project that has collected images of self-made video game avatars from trans-identifying video game players who identified some sort of connection to their player characters. This website hosts a variety of visualizations for the data attached to the submissions contained within that archive. These visualizations provide an overview of the demographics and experiences represented within the archive’s collection.

Submit to the Archive!
Trans-identifying gamers can submit to the archive in a survey here.
